title: What's up with competitive eating?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss competitive eating: its origins in the Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest on Coney Island (rumored 1916 patriotism challenge), early stunts like Ping Bodie's spaghetti contest with an ostrich, the rise of the International Federation of Competitive Eating (IFOCE, later Major League Eating), champions Takeru Kobayashi and Joey Chestnut, Sonya "Black Widow" Thomas's records, rules such as the no-vomit-on-table "Roman incident" and water dunking, training methods and health dangers (water intoxication, gastroparesis), theories about stomach expansion and body fat, and Ed Cratchy's rejected paper. The episode closes with listener mail from Sarah about being banned from listening to the podcast in her AP biology class, and ad reads for Altoids and the Camera.
topics: Ryan Reynolds Van Wilder competitive eating criticism

segments.title: Opening banter and buffet talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Josh's high school wing-eating days and buffets, then set up the topic of competitive eating.

segments.title: Origins of competitive eating
segments.summary: The hosts describe the IFOCE (later Major League Eating), founded by Nathan's publicity wing. They recount the rumored 1916 Coney Island hot dog challenge and the 1919 spaghetti contest between Ping Bodie and an ostrich, along with early county fair pie and painting contests.
topics: Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest origins

segments.title: Takeru Kobayashi and Joey Chestnut
segments.summary: Competitive eating grew in the late nineties and 2000s. Takeru Kobayashi dominated from about 2001 to 2006, and Joey Chestnut beat him in 2007 at Nathan's, with Kobayashi citing a jaw injury. Chestnut has since held many records.

segments.title: Sonya Thomas and records
segments.summary: The hosts list records held by Sonya Thomas, the 100-pound 'Black Widow,' including hard-boiled eggs, lobsters, and wings, and note her ranking as a top female eater.

segments.title: Rules, vomiting, and water dunking
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the rule that vomiting on the table or food disqualifies an eater (the 'Roman incident'), Kobayashi's 2002 vomit controversy, and the common practice of dunking buns in water. Josh shares a story of a birthday shot that made him vomit.

segments.title: Technique, training, and health dangers
segments.summary: Kobayashi's technique of breaking the hot dog and dunking the bun is described. Training methods such as drinking large amounts of water and fasting are covered, along with dangers including water intoxication, a fatal case, and gastroparesis. Theories about stomach stretch and body fat are mentioned, along with Ed Cratchy's paper that was rejected by a medical journal.

segments.title: Criticism and extreme food challenges
segments.summary: Ryan Reynolds is cited as a critic who sees competitive eating as a symbol of American waste. The hosts mention Leo Zornitsky's mayonnaise record and Kobayashi's cow brain record.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sarah about AP biology
segments.summary: Sarah writes that her AP biology teacher banned her iPod, on which she listened to the podcast during study hall, and she used episode facts in class.

segments.title: Sign-off and ads
segments.summary: The hosts close with a call for listener feedback and ad reads for Altoids and a camera.
